stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .74", "p = .066"), Sentence = c("All Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons were significant (Δz = 0.06-0.14, ps ≤ .008), except the comparison between the two persuasion conversations (Δz = 0.01, p = .74).", "Across the four complementarity predictors, the permutation test did not reach conventional significance, observed mean |r| = .111 versus a permuted mean of .068, p = .066." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: In this study, we examined how complementarity differs depending on the context of the conversation, including two conversations with persuasion roles.

Warmth complementarity has been associated with liking, positive affect, task performance, and relationship satisfaction (Halberstadt et al., 2023; Kurzius et al., 2022; Markey et al., 2010; Slotter et al., 2023), consistent with the idea that coordinated warmth enacts mutual responsiveness (Reis et al., 2004).

text.text: Evidence for dominance complementarity is mixed.

Observed indices have often shown weak or null associations with relationship evaluations (Cundiff et al., 2015; Slotter et al., 2023), and dominance levels and trajectories were unrelated to perceived conflict resolution in a recent CAID study (Gibson et al., 2024).

Thomas (2015), however, found that stronger moment-to-moment dominance reciprocity accompanied higher marital satisfaction.

text.text: Two further considerations bear on how complementarity should relate to satisfaction.

First, Orford (1986) argued that dominance invites submission mainly when interactions are warm, so any association between dominance reciprocity and satisfaction could depend on how warm a couple is.

text.text: Second, a warmth correspondence index pools two patterns that the couples literature treats as opposites: partners becoming warmer together and partners becoming colder together.
The latter resembles negative reciprocity, in which one partner's negativity is followed by the other's, a marker of distressed relationships (Gottman & Levenson, 1992; Ramos Salazar, 2015).

text.text: A pooled index could therefore obscure associations that run in opposite directions, and it is at best an INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY indirect indicator of mutual responsiveness.
We examined how complementarity is related to relationship satisfaction, expecting a positive association for moment-to-moment warmth complementarity and leaving dominance associations open.
We studied 137 Swiss romantic couples who completed four videotaped, 5-min conversations coded with CAID.
Couples discussed the best and worst aspects of their relationship and completed two persuasion conversations concerning a standing dietary disagreement.
In the persuasion conversations, each partner was assigned the persuasion role in turn.
Both partners also reported relationship satisfaction.
Because the study was not preregistered, we present theory-guided research questions (RQs) rather than confirmatory hypotheses.

For consistency (RQ1), we expected dominance complementarity to show stronger crossconversation consistency than warmth complementarity, replicating the pattern reported by Thomas (2015), and used generalizability analyses to distinguish stable couple differences from conversation and observer effects.

text.text: For context (RQ2), we expected warmth complementarity to be strongest during the positive relationship conversation and dominance complementarity to be strongest when influence was contested (RQ2a).
We also expected assigned persuasion roles to reverse which partner was more dominant, without predicting whether role assignment would change the strength of dominance complementarity itself (RQ2b).
For satisfaction (RQ3), we expected stronger moment-to-moment warmth complementarity to be associated with greater relationship satisfaction and treated dominance associations as open questions.
Exploratory analyses extended RQ3.

One tested whether warmth moderates the dominance association, as Orford's (1986) proposal implies, and another separated warmth correspondence in warm INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY moments from correspondence in cold moments.

Couples were recruited through online and community advertisements in the Zürich region.
Eligibility required that both partners were adults in a romantic relationship, regularly shared meals, and differed in their habitual consumption of meat or other animal products.
Cohabitation was not required, although couples had to share at least one meal per day.
Of the 617 individuals who began the baseline survey, 339 completed it and 142 couples attended the laboratory session.
Five couples completed the laboratory session in English and therefore could not be coded with the German-language observational protocol, yielding a final sample of 137 couples (274 individuals).
Baseline questionnaire data were available for 270 participants.
Participants averaged 23.87 years of age (SD = 6.82, range = 18-67); 52.8% identified as women and 47.2% as men.
Most couples were mixed gender (93.2%).

The sample was relatively highly educated, with most participants holding either a Swiss academic secondary diploma (53.7%) or a university degree (28.1%) and was predominantly politically left of center.
Consistent with the parent study, couples differed in their consumption of animal products.
On a 1--9 meat-frequency item, lower-animal-consuming partners averaged 2.06 (SD = 1.26), whereas higher-animal-consuming partners averaged 4.68 (SD = 1.83).
Dietary role was strongly gendered: 85.3% of lower-animal-consuming partners were women.

Six couples could not be classified unambiguously using the parent-study algorithm, which combined standardized baseline meat and fish frequencies with the standardized proportion of diary meals containing meat or fish (Tan et al., 2025) and were excluded only from analyses requiring this dietary-role assignment.

Because the study was embedded within a larger project, no a priori power analysis was conducted for the present questions.

A sensitivity analysis indicated that 137 couples provided 80% power to detect approximately r = .24 (α = .05, two-tailed), comparable to previously reported associations between warmth complementarity and relationship outcomes.
Couples attended a single laboratory session, provided written informed consent, and completed four video-recorded 5-min conversations while alone in the laboratory.
Conversation order was randomized.

Topics included the best aspects of the relationship, the most challenging aspects of the relationship, a discussion in which the lower-animal-consuming partner argued that the other partner should eat less meat, and a second discussion in which the higher-animalconsuming partner argued that the other partner should eat more meat.
Participants were instructed to interact as naturally as they would at home.
The two persuasion conversations therefore experimentally manipulated which partner occupied the persuasion role while maintaining an otherwise observational, within-couple design.
All materials were administered in German.
Participants were compensated CHF 120 for completing the full Partner Diet Study protocol.
Interactions were coded using the Continuous Assessment of Interpersonal Dynamics (CAID; Lizdek et al., 2012; Sadler et al., 2009) implemented in DARMA (Girard & Wright, 2018).

Each recording was coded by four observers, except for one recording coded by three.
The first and last 10 s of each recording were removed to minimize instruction lag and recording artifacts.
Indices computed with 5-s trimming correlated .99 with those used here, and the satisfaction estimates for the moment-to-moment indices were essentially unchanged (Section S2).
Momentary composite series were calculated by averaging observer ratings at each time point, requiring at least two observer streams.

Twenty-three observer streams (0.5%) whose ratings, after linear trends were removed, showed negative average agreement with the remaining observers of the same recording were excluded, consistent with screening in previous CAID work, although our criterion was more conservative, excluding only clearly aberrant streams.
Without these exclusions, indices correlated .97 or higher with the screened indices and satisfaction estimates were essentially unchanged (Section S2).
Following exclusions, 1,071 recordings were represented by four observer streams, 22 by three streams, and one by two streams.
Mean coefficient alpha across recordings was .79 for dominance and .40 for warmth, with lower observer agreement for warmth consistent with previous CAID studies.
Agreement for dominance was stable across the months of coding, whereas agreement for warmth was lower for recordings coded later in the period (Section S7).
The consequences of this level of INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY agreement for the reliability of the complementarity indices were evaluated directly through the generalizability analyses.
For moment-to-moment analyses, each composite time series was linearly detrended within person and conversation so that shared linear trends could not inflate the moment-tomoment indices.
Means and within-conversation variability were calculated from the trimmed, undetrended series.

Across conversations, both partners behaved relatively warmly.

Mean warmth was 124 for lower-animal-consuming partners and 129 for higher-animal-consuming partners on the -1,000 to +1,000 scale, with the highest values occurring during the discussion of the best aspects of the relationship.
Average dominance remained near the midpoint of the scale, although substantial within-conversation variability (SD ≈ 190) indicated frequent shifts between leading and yielding.
Complementarity was evident across all conversations.
Partners' detrended warmth trajectories were positively correlated (M = .26, SD = .11), whereas detrended dominance trajectories were strongly negatively correlated (M = -.73, SD = .14).

In contrast, randomly repaired pseudo-couples showed essentially no complementarity (warmth M = .00; dominance M = -.02), indicating that the observed coordination reflected genuine interpersonal processes within couples rather than shared responses to the task structure.
Complementarity was also present from the first minute and remained broadly stable within each conversation (Section S8).
Dominance reciprocity was concentrated in slow cycles (Section S10).
Cycles longer than 60 s contributed 53% of the moment-to-moment correlation, cycles of 30 to 60 s contributed 24%, and cycles of 10 to 30 s contributed 19%.
Cycles of 10 s or shorter contributed only 5%.
Reciprocity grew stronger as the timescale lengthened, from -.32 for the fastest cycles to -.81 for the slowest.

The correlation between one partner's dominance and the other's dominance a few seconds earlier declined smoothly as the time offset increased and reached zero at about 20 s, whereas warmth correspondence fell off more quickly and carried more of its variance in short cycles.
An index computed from cycles longer than 30 s alone correlated .96 with the full index and was consistent across conversations (α = .69).
Like the full index reported below, it was unrelated to satisfaction (B = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.14]).

The concentration of reciprocity in slow cycles parallels Sadler et al. (2009), whose spectral analyses placed couples' shared dominance cycles at periods of about 1.5 to 3.3 min and excluded cycles shorter than 30 s.

Momentto-moment dominance complementarity demonstrated strong consistency across conversations (α = .79, ICC(2,k) = .76), with a single-conversation ICC(2,1) of .45.
Moment-to-moment warmth complementarity was less consistent (α = .55, ICC(2,k) = .52), with a single-conversation ICC(2,1) of .21.

Similarity in partners' average warmth was highly consistent across conversations (α = .80), whereas mean-level dominance complementarity was somewhat less consistent (α = .66).
Generalizability analyses clarified these findings.
For moment-to-moment dominance complementarity, stable between-couple differences accounted for a substantial proportion of the reliable variance.
A single conversation coded by four observers yielded good reliability for estimating a couple's standing in that conversation (R 1F = .83).
Reliability increased for the fourconversation composite (R KF = .98; projected using the full 10-observer pool) and remained substantial when generalizing to new conversations (R 1R = .74).

The corresponding coefficients INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY for moment-to-moment warmth complementarity were considerably lower (R 1F = .26, R KF = .71, R 1R = .22), and the couple × conversation component (8.0% of variance) exceeded the couple component (2.4%), although both were small relative to observer and residual variance (Section S4).
This pattern closely matched previous CAID variance decompositions (Section S9).
Generalizability analyses also indicated reliable individual differences in contextual change.
Couple-specific change across conversations was highly reliable for dominance complementarity (R C = .90) and moderately reliable for warmth complementarity (R C = .60).

Interpersonal theory proposes that social behavior reflects an ongoing process of mutual influence in which each person's behavior shapes and is shaped by the other (Carson, 1969; Kiesler, 1983; Sadler et al., 2009).

text.text: Complementarity is one of the defining principles of these exchanges, but whether it is a stable characteristic of couples or a process that changes from one interaction to the next has rarely been tested.
We examined it across four conversations that differed in emotional tone and interpersonal demands.
The answer depended on the dimension.
Dominance complementarity generalized across conversations, whereas warmth complementarity varied systematically with conversational context.
Only warmth complementarity was associated with relationship satisfaction.

Mean-level indices showed a different pattern of consistency and did not predict satisfaction, so average interpersonal position and moment-to-moment coordination capture different aspects of how couples interact.
Interpersonal complementarity is both a stable dyadic characteristic and a situational process, and the balance between the two depends on the interpersonal dimension.
One possible reason for this difference is that dominance and warmth solve different interpersonal problems.
Reciprocal regulation of influence may provide relationships with a stable organizational structure that allows partners to negotiate decisions efficiently across situations.

In contrast, communal behavior may function primarily to communicate responsiveness to immediate relational needs, so that sensitivity to context, rather than consistency, may be its characteristic form.
Although speculative, this perspective suggests that different interpersonal dimensions may have evolved to balance stability and flexibility in different ways.
One implication of these findings is that stable interactional tendencies may exist at the level of the relationship rather than solely within individuals.
Personality psychology has largely moved beyond asking whether behavior is stable across situations.

Instead, contemporary perspectives emphasize that individuals display characteristic patterns of behavior across varying contexts, with stability emerging from recurring patterns rather than identical actions (Fleeson, 2001; Fleeson & Noftle, 2008).

text.text: The same framework fits dyads.

Couples differed reliably in the extent to which they exhibited reciprocal exchanges of dominance and submission, and these differences generalized across conversations despite substantial changes in the topics discussed and the roles partners occupied.
Rather than behaving identically across situations, couples appeared to maintain characteristic ways of organizing influence within their interactions.
Dominance complementarity may be an interactional analogue of a personality trait, a behavioral signature that recurs across situations.
The persuasion conversations make this point directly.
During these discussions, partners explicitly exchanged persuasion roles, producing large shifts in who occupied the dominant interpersonal position.
Dominance complementarity nevertheless remained consistent.
Studies of complementarity have rarely separated interpersonal position from interpersonal process.
Individuals may move to very different locations within interpersonal space depending on situational demands, yet still coordinate their behavior according to stable interpersonal principles.
The present findings suggest that reciprocal influence may represent one such principle.

Whether one partner led because they possessed greater expertise, held the assigned persuasion role, or simply initiated discussion, the broader process through which partners coordinated dominance and submission remained comparatively stable.
Complementarity therefore reflects more than similarity in observable behavior; it captures how partners regulate influence across situations.
The persuasion conversations also bear on Orford's (1986) proposal that hostile dominance provokes dominance rather than submission.

text.text: Reciprocity was strongest in the persuasion conversations, which were also the least warm, and within conversations it was not significantly weaker during mutually cold moments than during mutually warm ones.
As Thomas (2015) noted, Orford's review drew largely on complementarity aggregated over whole interactions, and the moment-level evidence here does not show the breakdown of reciprocity he described.

Because mutually cold moments occupied only a small fraction of these conversations, however, the test has limited power, and couples whose interactions tend to be cold may still show the pattern he proposed.
Perhaps the most theoretically informative finding concerned warmth complementarity.

Generalizability analyses suggested that part of the variability in warmth complementarity arose from systematic interactions between particular couples and particular conversational contexts, although the variance attributable to observers and to residual error was larger.

The same pattern appeared in earlier CAID generalizability studies, where the couple × conversation component for warmth was two to four times the couple component (Fox et al., 2021; Ramer et al., 2023;  Table S10).

text.text: These findings show both that warmth and warmth complementarity tend to be less reliable in CAID data and that couples reliably differed in how their warmth coordination changed across situations.
Substantively, the results suggest that communal coordination is more context-sensitive than dominance reciprocity.
Whereas reciprocal influence may constitute a relatively stable organizational feature of dyadic interaction across situations, warmth coordination appears to shift with relational demands.
The conversation effects fit this account.
Warmth complementarity was highest when partners discussed the best aspects of their relationship and lowest during the persuasion conversations.
These contexts differed in emotional valence and in the goals they imposed.

Positive relationship discussions encouraged mutual validation and shared emotional engagement, whereas persuasion required partners to advocate competing positions while maintaining the relationship.
Successful interpersonal functioning may therefore involve the capacity to adjust communal behavior appropriately as conversational demands change.
Whether such variability is adaptive remains an open question.
Couples whose warmth complementarity varied more across conversations were no more satisfied than couples whose complementarity was steadier (Section S13).
The satisfaction findings point the same way.
Only moment-to-moment warmth complementarity predicted satisfaction, and this association remained after controlling for couples' average warmth.
Average warmth reflects how positively partners behave toward one another overall, whereas warmth complementarity reflects how effectively partners coordinate those behaviors over time.
Satisfaction was associated with how closely partners coordinated warmth, over and above how warm they were.
Relationship research has long treated responsiveness and coordinated emotional exchange as central to satisfying relationships (Gottman & Levenson, 1992; Reis et al., 2004).

text.text: One possible explanation is that reciprocal influence is primarily an organizational feature of interaction rather than a determinant of relationship quality.
Most couples may settle into a stable way of negotiating influence, and many different arrangements may work equally well.
If so, couples differ in the form their coordination takes rather than in how well it works.
Whether reciprocity also carries evaluative weight may depend on the power difference between partners.

If so, reciprocity should be tied more closely to outcomes of the conversation itself than to global evaluations of the relationship.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the sample consisted primarily of young, German-speaking couples who differed in animal-product consumption and were willing to participate in an intensive observational study.

Although the diversity of conversation topics increases confidence that the findings are not specific to a single interaction, replication in older couples, couples experiencing greater relationship distress, and more culturally diverse samples will be important.
In addition, dietary role was confounded with gender (85.3% of lower-animal-consuming partners were women), so role-specific effects cannot be separated from gender effects.

Interpersonal coordination is also likely to be shaped by shared INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY history, by cultural norms regarding emotional expression and power, and by relationship duration, which was not assessed here.

Duration may matter more for dominance than for warmth: in 180 couples, dominance complementarity rose steeply over the first years of a relationship and then leveled off, whereas warmth complementarity did not change with duration (Slotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Duration may matter more for dominance than for warmth: in 180 couples, dominance complementarity rose steeply over the first years of a relationship and then leveled off, whereas warmth complementarity did not change with duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Slotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the laboratory conversations represent only a small sample of couples' everyday interactions.

They differed substantially in interpersonal demands and included an experimentally manipulated disagreement, but everyday relationships unfold across a far broader range of situations than a laboratory can recreate.

Recent developments in ambulatory assessment, passive sensing, and repeated observational methods provide an opportunity to examine complementarity across hundreds or even thousands of naturally occurring interactions.
Such designs would estimate dyadic signatures more precisely and identify the contexts that strengthen or weaken coordination.

Practically, researchers interested in dominance complementarity may obtain usable estimates from a single well-sampled interaction (ICC = .45 for one conversation vs. .76 for four), whereas assessing warmth complementarity requires sampling multiple interpersonal contexts.
Third, although the present findings demonstrate that complementarity varies systematically across contexts, they do not explain why this occurs.
The observed changes may reflect characteristics of the situation, stable individual differences, properties of the relationship, or interactions among all three.
For example, some couples may become more interpersonally coordinated under conditions of stress, whereas others may lose coordination.

Similarly, personality traits, attachment styles, conflict resolution strategies, or relationship goals may INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY influence both average levels of complementarity and the extent to which complementarity changes across situations.
Future research should examine these potential moderators directly.
Fourth, there are two potential limitations related to the dominance findings.
The first is that dominance reciprocity may partly reflect the alternation of speaking turns.

The CAID protocol treats interrupting, holding the floor, and declining to speak as expressions of influence (Lizdek et al., 2012; Sadler et al., 2009), but who speaks when also depends on politeness, conversational habits, and the task instructions.

text.text: The next step is to model interpersonal dynamics as a property of relationships rather than only to estimate average levels of complementarity.
Contemporary personality theory increasingly conceptualizes personality as patterns of behavior expressed across situations rather than as static average tendencies (Kuper et al., 2024).

text.text: The same approach can be applied to dyads.
Relationships can be described by average behavior and by stable signatures of how partners regulate influence, coordinate affiliation, and adjust to changing contexts.
Such signatures could ultimately provide a richer description of relationship functioning than either self-report questionnaires or mean behavioral scores alone.
The same questions arise outside romantic relationships.

Complementarity has been studied in psychotherapy, friendships, parent-child interactions, and work teams, yet these INTERPERSONAL COMPLEMENTARITY literatures have generally focused on whether complementarity occurs rather than whether it represents a stable characteristic of particular dyads.
Stable interactional tendencies and systematic contextual adaptation are unlikely to be unique to romantic couples and may be a general property of enduring relationships.
Asking when coordination reflects stable dyadic organization and when it reflects adaptation to the situation would give these literatures a common question.
Personality psychologists spent decades debating whether behavior reflects enduring dispositions or situational influences.

That debate has largely been settled for individuals, but the parallel question for interpersonal processes, whether complementarity is a stable property of relationships or arises anew in each interaction, has remained open.

Much of the existing literature implicitly assumes that complementarity operates similarly across interpersonal dimensions.
Our results instead indicate that different dimensions occupy different positions along a continuum from stable interpersonal organization to context-sensitive interpersonal adaptation.

Dominance reciprocity appears to function primarily as a stable characteristic of relationships, whereas warmth complementarity appears to reflect a context-sensitive process that responds to changing interpersonal demands.
Future work may benefit from asking which forms of complementarity are expected to be stable and under what conditions.

Reciprocal patterns of dominance generalized across markedly different conversations, whereas warmth coordination varied systematically with conversational context while remaining associated with relationship satisfaction.
Future work should ask how couples are complementary: which aspects of their coordination hold across situations and which change with the demands of the moment.

Treating relationships as organized systems of mutual influence connects interpersonal theory with current views of personality, in which stability lies in characteristic patterns of change rather than in fixed behavior.
